newsitem.title: NORWAY: Activists protest at Norway's rising CO2 emissions.
newsitem.headline: Activists protest at Norway's rising CO2 emissions.

text.p: About 40 youth activists from environment groups around the world staged a noisy protest on Thursday outside the Norwegian parliament over planned increases in Norway's emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2) -- a so-called greenhouse gas.

Led by Amsterdam-based International Youth Climate Campaign, demonstrators first delivered a letter addressed to Prime Minister Thorbjoern Jagland accusing the oil-rich country of making "a mockery" of international talks aimed at forging a global pact to reduce emissions.

Environmentalists are upset over forecasts that Norway's CO2 emissions will steeply increase before the end of the decade, driven by higher production of the country's huge oil and gas reserves and plans to build the first gas-fired power stations.
Figures from the Norwegian Society for the Conservation of Nature, which opposes the plans, indicate that the plants alone would raise Norwegian emissions by 6.3 percent.

"Norway is in danger of becoming one of the principal climate destroyers," said Mark Ballard, coordinator of the demonstration, which drew campaigners from 22 countries, including the United States, New Zealand, Bulgaria and Brazil.

"Norway has a reputation for being outspoken on environmental issues and has criticised others in the past such as Britain for acid rain. But as we can see now, when it conflicts with their own interests they are not so reputable."

Environmental negotiators from more than 150 countries -- including Norway -- are currently working to hammer out a broad agreement on how best to reduce the world's output of CO2 and other gases blamed for the phenomenon known as global warming.
The aim is to reach consensus before a high-level December meeting in Kyoto, Japan, which it is hoped will yield a legally binding 10-year agreement with clear targets.

"Starting construction of these (gas) plants will show that Norway blatantly disrespects the spirit of these negotiations," the letter, addressed to Prime Minister Jagland and signed by 17 European environmental organisations, said.

"If the European Union can agree to reduce its emissions of carbon dioxide by 15 percent by 2010, Norway's plan to increase emissions by 30 percent during the same period makes a mockery of attempts by the global community to reach an agreement to halt the increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide levels."
The Norwegian government recently revised its prognosis for Norwegian CO2 emissions to 11.5 million tonnes in 1999, 24 percent up from a forecast last year of 9.3 million tonnes.

Apart from the gas-fired power stations, emissions are also set to rise from increased oil production, which is expected to hit around 3.7 million barrels per day (bpd) in 2000. That is 300,000 bpd higher than previous estimates.
